issues.legal_issue: A prosecution for instituting false, malicious, or vexatious legal proceedings requires more than a failure to prove the underlying allegation; the asserted falsehood or abuse must have the requisite wrongful intent and legal character.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that a second criminal writ petition sought the same relief as an earlier petition without disclosing the earlier petition and its dismissal.

The appellant said he was not well-versed in English and had been guided by his counsel; the counsel accepted responsibility for the omission, described it as inadvertent, and tendered an unconditional apology.
The first writ petition had been dismissed in limine and the second had been dismissed in default, rather than either dismissal establishing that the underlying allegations were false.
The High Court closed the contempt proceedings after the complainant chose not to pursue them further.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances alleged did not establish that the appellant had instituted a false, malicious, or vexatious proceeding, and the complaint did not make out the charged offence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1)(viii) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses proceedings that are false, malicious, or vexatious in the legally wrongful sense. A falsehood attracting criminal consequences requires the requisite intentional or knowing dishonesty; inability to prove a fact does not by itself make it false. Malice entails an intentional wrongful act without just cause or excuse, and a vexatious proceeding lacks a discernible legal basis and operates principally to harass. The Court relied on Masumsha Hasanasha Musalman v. State of Maharashtra; Commissioner of Sales Tax, Uttar Pradesh v. Sanjiv Fabrics; A. Abdul Rashid Khan v. P.A.K.A. Shahul Hamid; Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Girja Shankar Pant; West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray; and the authorities on mala fides cited in its judgment.

predicates.prosecution_for_instituting_false_malici: The case is a prosecution alleging that a person instituted false, malicious, or vexatious legal proceedings against a protected person.
predicates.proceedings_shown_to_be_intentionally_fa: The proceedings were shown to involve intentional or knowing falsehood, wrongful malice, or a lack of legal basis coupled with harassment.

issues.definition: When a prosecution of this kind does not show that the proceedings were intentionally false, malicious, or baselessly harassing, the offence is not made out.

issues.legal_issue: The court may quash a criminal complaint that renews an unsupported allegation already considered in contempt proceedings that were closed at the complainant’s request, where the complaint is an abuse of process in a genuine property dispute.
material_facts: The contempt proceedings concerned the same alleged nondisclosure in the second writ petition and were closed after the complainant said he did not wish to pursue the remedy further.
The complaint under the Act was later based on that same alleged nondisclosure.
The parties had a continuing dispute over rights and possession of land, and the complainant had pursued criminal and revenue proceedings concerning it.

The record did not establish the intentional falsehood, malice, or vexatiousness required for the charged offence; the Court characterized the resort to proceedings as intimidatory and found no justification for launching the criminal prosecution afresh.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the lower courts’ orders, restored the Magistrate’s order, and quashed the complaint under the Act as an unjustified continuation of criminal process.
issues.legal_principle: The inherent power to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice permits quashing a wholly untenable criminal complaint and prevents needless harassment through criminal prosecution. Issue estoppel prevents relitigation of an identical issue of fact determined between the same parties, but the Court noted that the contempt order did not record a finding on the alleged false affidavit; it relied instead on the circumstances of the closure, the absence of the offence’s essential basis, and the abuse of process. A second complaint is not invariably barred, but is not maintainable where the earlier matter was disposed of after full consideration on the merits. The Court relied on Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; Manipur Administration v. Thokchom Bira Singh and other issue-estoppel authorities cited in the judgment; Shiv Shankar Singh v. State of Bihar; Chandrapal Singh v. Maharaj Singh; and the authorities on binding judgments cited in its judgment.
